discovery: Atomic force microscopy with sub-molecular resolution: the qPlus sensor and functionalized-tip imaging of individual chemical bonds
subfield: Condensed matter physics / surface science and scanning probe microscopy
motivation: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor, a stiff quartz tuning-fork force detector that allows non-contact atomic force microscopy at small amplitudes and atomic resolution. Gross and Meyer then made a decisive step by terminating the tip with a single CO molecule. In 2009 this let them image the chemical-bond skeleton of individual molecules in real space for the first time. Together these advances turned the chemical bond from an inferred concept into something directly seen. The technique has since resolved bond orders, on-surface reaction products, single-molecule charge states and, in our own laboratories, individual hydrogen bonds and the structure of two-dimensional ice. It is a true '0 to 1' instrument advance. It probes forces rather than only electronic states, reaches light atoms such as hydrogen that tunnelling microscopy misses, and has become an indispensable tool across physics, chemistry and materials science worldwide.
